Passers-by and entrepreneurs are being intimidated by a group of young people between 10 and 17 years old. That is why the municipality of Hoogeveen is intervening. Mayor <entity id="person:martijn-breukelman">Martijn Breukelman</entity> is designating a safety risk area with effect from today after evenings of unrest, in order to be able to carry out preventive searches. The cameras that were installed a few days ago had not yet had the desired effect. Nor had the ban on assembly. The municipality is not entirely clear about where the unrest comes from. Boredom may play a role. "But it concerns behaviour that we absolutely do not accept", mayor Breukelman emphasises. That is why the municipality has had enough: "The time for consultation is over, we are now taking firm action." Unsafe For entrepreneurs and residents, the situation has become untenable. Erwin Slomp, chairman of Stichting Binnenstad Hoogeveen, sees how the retail climate is suffering from the unrest. "People no longer feel safe when cobras or other fireworks are thrown at them. Shopkeepers and their staff are being intimidated and visitors no longer dare to enter the Hoofdstraat. This is a line that has been crossed." In recent evenings, several young people were pulled off their fatbikes by police, detained or fined. During searches, police found not only fireworks, but also knives and knuckledusters. Almost all of them are minors, so police will also talk to the parents. 'Dead village' According to the youths in the centre this afternoon, the rioters' motive is mainly a combination of boredom, group pressure and a craving for sensation. "People just want to act tough and show that they are mafia," says a 15-year-old boy on a fatbike. "They just want to fight with the police." A blond boy of just 13 years old says that the boys causing nuisance in the evenings know each other from Hoogeveen. They come from different schools. In online groups they urge each other to come too. "Finally something is happening in this dead village. When everyone is there, it is fun. Now it is mainly provoking the police with fireworks and then driving away as fast as possible." He does understand that the situation is getting out of hand: "My parents find it awful. I am still allowed to meet up in the evening but actually not to come to the centre anymore." A question about whether he will listen to his parents is answered only with a smile. Call to parents Together with the <entity id="org:openbaar-ministerie">Openbaar Ministerie</entity>, the municipality is mapping the identity of the troublemakers. More than 65 names are already known. Their parents can all expect a letter. Both the mayor and the city centre association explicitly point to the role of the guardians. Breukelman: "14- or 15-year-olds with knives or knuckledusters, that is no longer mischief." And Slomp also makes an urgent appeal to parents: "Know where your child hangs out in the evening and what it does. There is also a responsibility of your own there."

title: Suspect in Herkenbosch murder now also suspected of murdering his own mother
lead: Daniel B., the German man suspected of the murder of Paul Vossen from Herkenbosch in Limburg, is now also suspected of murdering his mother. The justice authorities announced this this afternoon in the court in <entity id="org:gemeente-roermond">Roermond</entity>. The woman has been missing for almost two years. Police and justice authorities already had "strong indications" that B. had something to do with his mother's disappearance, but not enough for a formal suspicion of murder. Now that is therefore different. The Public Prosecution Service has not disclosed what new evidence or leads there are. The 48-year-old B. was questioned last month about his mother's disappearance. In a storage space in the German municipality of Heinsberg, items with the woman's blood were previously found. In another storage space, which was in her name, there were shovels and a rake. The woman had no garden of her own. The police suspect that the items were used to bury the woman. B. denies all involvement in her disappearance. He also says he has nothing to do with the death of Paul Vossen. Home robbery Daniel B. was arrested in September last year on suspicion of the murder of Vossen, earlier that month. The OM thinks that the man was killed during a failed home robbery. Vossen (66) had just retired and was found with severe injuries in the garden of his villa in Herkenbosch. He died shortly afterwards. B. lived not far from Herkenbosch at that time. The apartment in Montfort where he was arrested was in the name of his mother Teresa Krug. The woman of Polish origin had not been seen since March 2025, but was never reported missing. Searches for her body have so far yielded nothing. The two cases are being handled simultaneously, writes L1 Nieuws . That will probably happen next year.

title: Ten injured in stabbing at school in Poland, suspect (19) arrested
lead: Ten people were injured in a stabbing at a school for vocational education in the north of Poland. A 19-year-old student of the school could be arrested in the vicinity. The injured are five students, two teachers, two bystanders and the perpetrator. The latter injured himself, local authorities report. No one is in life-threatening danger. One person did sustain serious injuries and a number of victims were taken to a hospital by helicopter. The attack with a "sharp object" took place around 11:00 in Ostroleka, about 120 kilometers northeast of Warsaw. The authorities have not disclosed anything about a possible motive. The police shared a photo of the arrest: The suspect could be detained less than a kilometer from the school, after he had fled. He was taken to the hospital with unknown injuries. Two hours after the attack, the mayor of Ostroleka announced that the school will remain closed, so that the authorities can investigate the site of the attack.

title: Extensive mortgage fraud by criminals, report has been lying in a drawer for months
lead: In recent years, between 6,000 and 11,000 homes in the Netherlands have been bought with forged papers. By committing fraud when applying for the mortgage, criminals manage to get the homes into their hands in order to carry out illegal activities there. That is stated in a not yet published report that, according to insiders, has been lying at the Ministry of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-justitie-en-veiligheid">Justitie en Veiligheid</entity> for more than six months. The report was drawn up by the Financial Expertise Centre, which was given the assignment by the previous <entity id="org:kabinet">kabinet</entity> to conduct research into the "nature and extent" of mortgage fraud in the Netherlands. Members of parliament, but also the Dutch Association of Banks (NVB) and the professional association of <entity id="org:zbo-notarissen">notarissen</entity>, have been very concerned about this form of fraud for some years. Criminals manage to buy properties with the help of, for example, forged payslips, employer statements, annual figures or tax returns. Undermining The purchased homes are used for "money laundering, illegal rental, labour exploitation, drug crime and other forms of undermining", said NVB chair Medy van der Laan today in <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity>. She was there for a hearing on undermining crime. The results of the report, which was supposed to be ready in March, have been awaited for months. "Mortgage fraud is increasingly taking place," said Van der Laan. "Exploitation is taking place, deception and other very terrible things. And it disrupts the livability of a neighbourhood." In 2024, reports already emerged via Het Financieele Dagblad about a criminal network that bought hundreds of homes in the Amsterdam region between 2018 and 2023 through manipulation. Those properties turned out to have been used for, among other things, storage of money and drugs, and labour migrants were housed there. The fraudsters, mostly Bulgarian labour migrants, had been hired by administrative offices to forge payslips. In the Tweede Kamer, among others, VVD and NSC asked questions about it to the then cabinet. Pro has also long been urging measures. The Royal Dutch Association of Civil-law Notaries (KNB) also points to "flawed legislation" and "limited possibilities for information exchange". Checking with the tax authority Just like banks, notaries would like the possibility to verify income data with the <entity id="org:belastingdienst">Belastingdienst</entity>. That should not be a problem. "We respect all sensitivities around privacy. For an application, we only want to check whether the data we have received are correct," said Van der Laan. MP Mutluer of Pro is urging that the report and the recommendations now be sent to the Kamer as quickly as possible. Next week, a debate on this subject is also scheduled.

title: 200,000 Yemenis flee due to reignited fighting
lead: The UN organization for migration and aid to refugees (IOM) is raising the alarm about the situation in Yemen. Since the reignition of the battle between the Houthis and the government army, at the beginning of last month, around 200,000 Yemenis have fled. "People are running for their lives but find safety nowhere," says IOM director Amy Pope. "They now need shelter, food and safety. Our people are on the ground, but the funding is not." Pope is asking donor countries to take action. "Yemen must not become a forgotten crisis. The world has the means to help. They must be used now." Nearly thirteen years For many refugees, it is not the first time they have had to leave their place of residence. The civil war in Yemen has already lasted more than thirteen years. It began with an uprising by the Iran-backed Houthis. The government army has the support of Saudi Arabia. Through UN mediation, a ceasefire was reached in 2022. That was broken last month by an offensive by the Houthis. They gained control of the entire area along the Red Sea. From there, airports, military complexes and oil installations in Saudi Arabia are being fired upon with rockets and drones, again today as well. The conquests increase the Houthis' ability to fire on shipping traffic in the Strait of Bab al-Mandab, the connection between the Gulf of Aden and the Red Sea. Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government army have begun a counteroffensive to push back the Houthis. The fighting is currently taking place mainly near the town of Dhubab on the Red Sea and in the area south of the city of Ta'izz. These are images from Monday of the government army's offensive near the Strait of Bab el-Mandeb:

title: House of Representatives in favour of alcohol meter for convicted persons
lead: A majority of the House of Representatives supports the introduction of the alcohol meter. That is an ankle bracelet for people who have been convicted of a crime in which alcohol played a role, and who have been given an alcohol ban by the court. It can involve, for example, a traffic accident or domestic violence. The alcohol meter absorbs skin moisture and sweat and detects whether alcohol is present in it. The probation service receives a notification upon alcohol intake and contacts this person. If it has been established that the person has indeed been drinking, and that it was for example not cleaning agent that someone was working with, then a warning follows. Pilots The law has already been prepared by previous cabinets but is only now before the House. The alcohol meter was tested in pilots in which convicted persons could voluntarily choose the ankle bracelet instead of urine and blood tests. In 2023, nearly 1500 people were given an alcohol ban or an alcohol and drugs ban. Of the people with an alcohol meter, 10 percent committed an offence while wearing the ankle bracelet, compared to 51 percent of the persons with only urine checks. These more positive effects were also present three months after disconnecting the ankle bracelet, according to police figures. Not refusing A refusal to wear the alcohol meter while the court has prescribed an alcohol ban is regarded as refusing a punishment. This also applies to attempts to remove the ankle bracelet. Alcohol meters cost around 1500 euros. In case of destruction or loss, the wearer must pay the costs. Unlike an ankle bracelet, an alcohol meter cannot track where someone is.

title: 'Drifting' motorcyclist gets community service for fatal accident in Lelystad
lead: A motorcyclist who caused a fatal accident in Lelystad two years ago has been sentenced to 240 hours of community service. The 32-year-old man must also pay 37,000 euros in damages to the victim's parents. The accident happened on 2 June 2024 on the Karperweg in Lelystad during an illegal 'drift' event. Hundreds of spectators were present. When drifting on a motorcycle, the rider deliberately loses grip on the rear wheel and the rear wheel slides sideways through the bend. The motorcyclist from Schiedam ended up on the wrong side of the road and collided head-on with a cross motorcycle. The 18-year-old rider of that motorcycle from Maarssen died two days later from his injuries, writes Omroep Flevoland . Motorcycles gone The <entity id="org:openbaar-ministerie">Openbaar Ministerie</entity> had demanded eight months in prison. The court arrives at a much lower sentence, partly because the man from Schiedam had no criminal record and has expressed regret. After the fatal accident, the man got rid of his motorcycles and says he never wants to ride a motorcycle again. According to the judge, the man was careless and inattentive, but not reckless. The court writes in the verdict that the suspect, although fatal, in fact violated one traffic rule: not keeping sufficiently to the right. According to the OM, there was an illegal street race, but the judge does not agree. Participants did drift, but according to the court it was not about speed. A 36-year-old man from Rotterdam who according to the OM was the organizer of the drift event has been acquitted of manslaughter. According to the court, he did not organize an illegal street race and it cannot be established with certainty whether he gave the starting signal for the drift with the fatal outcome.

title: Couple in US charged with abuse in 'horror house' full of surrogate children
lead: A couple from California has been charged in a case involving the abuse of at least fifteen children between the ages of two months and thirteen years. Fourteen of the children are said to have been born via surrogacy. According to prosecutors, the children were beaten and punched by nannies in the couple's villa. Guojun Xuan (66) and Silvia Zhang (39) kept most of the children in their villa in Arcadia, about 20 kilometers from Los Angeles. The children were taken in at their home and cared for by nannies, prosecutors stated. They are said to have spent hours a day in three different rooms of the villa, so-called 'learning centers', where the nannies supervised. Last year, 32 surveillance cameras were found in the villa. According to the prosecution, the couple used them to keep an eye on the nannies. Footage recorded how they systematically beat and harshly punished the children. The couple is accused of having recruited women to become surrogates and of having conspired to have the children abused. Prosecutor Nathan Hochman called the villa a "horror house". "The number of children exposed to this alleged horrific abuse is unprecedented," he said. The couple was arrested yesterday and says it is innocent. According to American media, they wanted to create a large family. Head injury The investigation started after a two-month-old baby with head injuries was brought into the hospital, in July last year . One of the nannies is said to have hit the newborn baby on the head. Hospital staff did not trust it and notified the police. An arrest warrant was already issued for the nanny last year, but she is said to still be on the run. 21 children who were under the couple's supervision were placed elsewhere: fifteen were removed from the villa and six were elsewhere. Most of the children were between one and three years old. The couple was already detained at the time, because they are said to have known that their baby was injured and did not raise the alarm. The couple was released on bail because no formal charge had yet been filed. Now that the Public Prosecution Service and the police have completed the investigation, the two could be arrested again. Surrogates In addition to the abuse, the couple is also suspected of making false statements to at least two women who became surrogates. Zhang is said to have said that she had difficulty getting pregnant. Prosecutors expect that the surrogates came from different parts of the United States and that they did not know that others were also carrying embryos for the two.

title: Police in Bavaria searching for a puma or something that looks like one
lead: A municipality close to Munich Airport in the German state of Bavaria is calling on residents to be careful because a wild feline animal has been sighted. It may be a puma. The police have launched a large search operation. A helicopter and drones have been deployed. The animal was spotted last night by a hunter with night-vision equipment. That was in the Notzinger Moos nature reserve, a few kilometres from the airport. He made a video of it. The images were viewed by experts last night and they concluded that it may be a puma. No panic The municipality of Erding, which sent the warning out into the world, does not want to cause panic. "We want to make sure that people keep a slightly better eye on their surroundings," a spokesperson told regional broadcaster BR . Anyone who sees the animal or knows where it is staying should not go towards it but call the police immediately. Dog owners are advised to keep their dog on a leash. "And do not let your small children play outside unsupervised," the spokesperson said. Puma and lion It would not be the first time that an animal in Germany was mistaken for a puma or lion. Last year, a search operation for a puma was also launched in the state of Saxony-Anhalt. It was not found. According to an expert, it must have been a cat. In 2023, police in Berlin spent 30 hours searching for a lion that was said to have escaped. That one was not found either. It was presumably a wild boar.

title: Nieuw-Lekkerland defaced in many places with swastika in flag of Israel
lead: In Nieuw-Lekkerland in the <entity id="org:provincie-zuid-holland">provincie Zuid-Holland</entity>, defacements with swastikas have been found in dozens of places. The municipality is filing a report. Het Reformatorisch Dagblad reported earlier about the defacements. In images shared by the newspaper, paving stones can be seen on which Israeli flags have been sprayed with a paint spray can. In the places where the Star of David should be, there is a swastika. The graffiti is being removed. Possibly a number of tiles will have to be replaced. Mayor <entity id="person:theo-segers">Theo Segers</entity> of the <entity id="org:gemeente-molenlanden">gemeente Molenlanden</entity>, under which Nieuw-Lekkerland falls, calls the defacements to news agency ANP "very reprehensible". Not the first time According to the municipality, the swastikas were applied last night. A spokesperson reports that defacements have now been removed at approximately thirty locations. "Possibly they will be found in even more places." The municipality expects everything to be cleaned up tomorrow. It is not the first time that swastikas have been applied in the public space of Nieuw-Lekkerland. That also happened earlier this year. At that time, street furniture and bus shelters were defaced because of the possible arrival of an asylum seekers' centre. A resident of the place then decided to stick stickers with hearts on the swastikas : It is exactly three years ago today that the terrorist organisation Hamas carried out a major attack on Israel. More than 1200 people were killed and 251 people were taken hostage. Today, the attacks by Hamas are commemorated in many places around the world, including in the Netherlands, among others in <entity id="org:gemeente-s-gravenhage">Den Haag</entity> and <entity id="org:gemeente-amsterdam">Amsterdam</entity>.

title: Mayor of Oldebroek at Coming Out Day celebration after council scrapping lgbti policy
lead: Oldebroek hoists the rainbow flag on Coming Out Day, but not at the town hall. The Christian-conservative council of the Veluwe municipality decided last week officially to stop lgbti policy and no longer hoist the rainbow flag. That was already in the coalition agreement of the Christelijk Verbond Oldebroek (CVO), the SGP and Algemeen Belang Oldebroek (ABO). At the Kruiskerk the rainbow flag will indeed flutter on Saturday. And mayor <entity id="person:tanja-haseloop-amsing">Tanja Haseloop-Amsing</entity> will be present when the flag is hoisted, although the council decided to continue "without woke expressions". Haseloop-Amsing (VVD) says to Omroep <entity id="org:provincie-gelderland">Gelderland</entity> that she is not only chair of the college of mayor and aldermen, but that she has her own role and her own line. "As mayor I am also an independent administrative body, which must keep an eye on the fact that in this village we also still treat each other reasonably well. That there is administrative integrity. That role as mother of the municipality I now take on." Flag action Reverend Han Wilmink of the Kruiskerk will hoist the flag, just like every year. He thinks it is extra important this year. "This municipal policy gives people a sign: you do not belong. We must oppose and resist that." State secretary <entity id="person:claudia-van-bruggen">Claudia van Bruggen</entity> of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-justitie-en-veiligheid">Justitie en Veiligheid</entity>, who comes from the region, will also be there, Trouw writes. After the presentation of the coalition agreement in July, resident Kjeld Mooi decided to stand up against the plans of the municipal government to scrap the lgbti policy. At the installation of the council he stood with a rainbow flag in front of the town hall. He received much support for his action, including from lgbti people in the municipality who said that they always have to hide their orientation. Coming Out Day is on Sunday 11 October, but the organisation in Oldebroek is already holding the meeting on Saturday, out of respect for the Sunday rest. Everyone in the village who wants one can get a rainbow flag to hang out at home on Saturday. More than 250 flags have already been requested.

title: Temporary protection or asylum? Ukrainians do not really know where they stand
lead: Mixed feelings among Ukrainians after it became known that their asylum applications must be reviewed. "On the one hand there is slight hope that an end will come to the temporary nature of our stay, on the other hand we still do not know where we stand," says Ukrainian Jamal Statsenko. An experience that Anna Bieliaieva of Vital'nya, a community for Ukrainian refugees in the Netherlands, shares. "We increasingly hear that people are aware of the European ruling, but what will happen now remains unclear." The European Court of Justice ruled last week that the Netherlands must get to work on assessing the asylum applications of more than 140,000 Ukrainians. A problem for <entity id="org:kabinet">het kabinet</entity>, because the asylum system will thus come under even more pressure. 'Do we have to go back, or are we staying here?' For the Ukrainians who fled their country after the outbreak of the war, the Temporary Protection Directive was activated for the first time. A European rule devised to quickly offer temporary protection in a situation of a large influx of refugees. As a result, Ukrainians immediately received the right to shelter, work, medical care and education for the children. "Since the beginning of the war they have actually been in a very pleasant waiting room. But even if you are in a waiting room that is very comfortable, it remains a waiting room," says Mark Klaassen, assistant professor of immigration law at <entity id="org:gemeente-leiden">Leiden</entity> University. From Europe, the protection is extended time and again, by now until March 2028. But it remains the question what will happen after that. According to Ukrainians, that uncertainty is the big problem. "My son has lived half his life here. He speaks Dutch, has his social life with friends here," says Bieliaieva. "Lately he keeps asking which school he will go to after group 8. Do we have to go back, or are we still here? I cannot give an answer to that." Tidal wave of asylum applications The advantage of that special European rule is that an individual asylum procedure does not have to be completed. As a result, immigration services do not suddenly have to process an enormous number of applications. That is where the Netherlands went wrong. The rule has been worked out here in such a way that Ukrainians had to submit an asylum application, after which they received that temporary European protection. The asylum applications were then paused until the temporary protection expires. That is not allowed, the European Court now says: the asylum applications are separate from the temporary protection. Since the Netherlands had the Ukrainians submit such an application, those must also be reviewed. A headache file for the ministry. "Let alone for the <entity id="org:immigratie-en-naturalisatiedienst">IND</entity>, which currently has to deal with a backlog of more than 50,000 people waiting for a decision. On top of that, they see this tidal wave of assessments coming at them," says Klaassen. Ukrainians are now not building up a right of residence. "With an asylum status you build up years of residence, after five years you could in theory become Dutch. Those years do not count for Ukrainians now," says the assistant professor of immigration law. Uncertainty remains It will still take a while before Ukrainians hear anything about their asylum application. Asylum minister Van den Brink wants to first process the people who are arriving now, then work through the waiting list and after that the group of Ukrainians will have their turn. He does emphasise in a letter to the House today that the European ruling has no effect on the way in which the reception of Ukrainians by municipalities is currently organised. According to Statsenko, an asylum status would help him get his own home. "With temporary protection, the chance that you get a mortgage is very small. It is also much harder to rent; landlords make difficulties about that temporariness." It is not the case that all Ukrainians are waiting for such an asylum procedure, says Bieliaieva. "Of course there are people who would like to go back. We love Ukraine and of course we would preferably never have left." Until the ministry has worked out how it will concretely tackle this situation, it remains a waiting game. "I hope to finally get clarity for the future and not another temporary extension," says Statsenko. Bieliaieva also wants to get the opportunity to really build something here. "It would be nice if we know where we stand. But at its core not much changes. What this exactly means, we do not know."

title: Pro-Palestinian protest with expressions of support for Hamas in Amsterdam disbanded
lead: A pro-Palestinian protest on Dam Square in Amsterdam has been disbanded by <entity id="person:femke-halsema">burgemeester Halsema</entity>. At the demonstration, slogans were chanted such as 'long live the 7th of October', referring to the attacks by Hamas in Israel on 7 October 2023. Demonstrators also burned an Israeli flag. Protesters with face masks held up a large green banner on which the slogan 'we support Hamas' could be read. Men with scarves over their faces held a banner that said 'glory to our martyrs, victory to the resistance'. Law not violated The <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> looked at the expressions on Dam Square and judged that the texts on the banners do not violate the law. Asked whether such texts are not tasteless on the day that the massacre that Hamas committed in Israel three years ago is commemorated, one organizer responds: "Tasteless? I don't know. It is provocative and I do understand why people do it." The man is angry because of a law being drafted to make glorification of terrorism punishable. According to the man, the Netherlands should not see Hamas as a terrorist organization but as a political movement, and support for it should not become punishable. Demonstrators who walked on from Dam Square into the city wanted to go to the neighborhood where many Jewish buildings are located. The police prevented the group from going that way, after which the group continued protesting in front of the door of the Stopera, the city hall. There an Israeli flag was set on fire. Demonstration disbanded An estimated 150 demonstrators were present on Dam Square, about half of them then walked on into the city. At 20:15 the demonstration was disbanded on the orders of the mayor, because part of the demonstrators did not follow the instruction to go to the Stopera. Thereupon the protesters left the area. Mayor Halsema calls the expressions of support by the demonstrators at the National Monument on Dam Square "shocking and distasteful", but also says that they are not punishable and that intervention on Dam Square was therefore not possible.

title: Six arrests for theft of Renoir paintings in the south of France
lead: A month after the painting theft from the Renoir museum in the south of France, the French police have arrested six suspects. Among them are the two suspected burglars, French media report. The arrests were made in four different departments in the south and east of France. The six are suspected of, among other things, theft in an organised context. They have been transferred to Nice for questioning. On 8 September, four paintings by the famous French impressionist Pierre-Auguste Renoir were stolen from the Musée Renoir in Cagnes-sur-Mers. The two thieves left two paintings behind in the museum's garden during their escape. Most valuable paintings It is not yet clear whether the other two have already been found. It concerns the works Madame Colonna Romano and Jeune Femme au puits (Young woman at the well). The paintings were on loan from Musée d'Orsay in Paris. The thieves seemed well prepared. They entered around 06.00 in the morning via a glass door and took the canvases in less than 3 minutes. They were the four most valuable pieces of the museum. It was opened in 1960 in Renoir's last residence. When the police arrived there, it turned out that part of the fencing had been cut through, allowing the perpetrators to enter the grounds. Security footage later showed that the thieves had sawn through the anchoring of the paintings in the wall.

title: Face of Spanish housing protests Maricarmen Abascal (87) has died
lead: Maricarmen Abascal, the 87-year-old woman who became the face and namesake of the housing protests in Spain, has died. That has been announced by the Spanish tenants' union. Abascal was evicted from her house, where she had lived for seventy years. Due to a rent increase she could no longer afford her house. Her eviction was the direct cause of the protests in Spain. Many Spaniards cannot afford housing due to inflation and a shortage of housing. Especially in the cities Madrid, Barcelona and Valencia there is too little housing. The country also has a large shortage of social housing. It concerns less than 2 percent of the available supply, while the European average is 8 percent. Maricarmen quickly became the face of the housing crisis in Spain: At Abascal's eviction hundreds of demonstrators were present. They regarded it as a new low point in the country's housing crisis. The activists tried to stop the clearance, but the police dispersed them with tear gas. In the end the eviction was reversed and the woman could continue living in her house. Decrees adopted Yesterday the Spanish government approved two housing market decrees. The measures for rent caps, a temporary ban on evictions and restrictions on the purchase of homes by companies were, according to Prime Minister Sánchez, "based on pure common sense". He stated that opinion polls showed that a large majority of the population is in favour of intervention in the housing market. The same decrees were rejected by parliament last week. Sánchez then called early elections for 29 November. Due to the dissolution of parliament, the measures can now be introduced temporarily and subsequently submitted to a smaller permanent body of 69 parliamentarians that remains in place during the election period. There is sufficient support there to keep the measures in place. The decrees have also been named after Maricarmen Abascal. Prime Minister Sánchez has expressed his condolences to the surviving relatives after her death.

title: Climate change cause of rapid decline of chinstrap penguin on British island
lead: British scientists have established that the population of chinstrap penguins on a British island in the southern Atlantic Ocean has declined dramatically. In 2011, 900,000 chinstrap penguins and 90,000 macaroni penguins lived on Zavodovski Island. Fourteen years later, the number of chinstrap penguins had fallen by 63 percent, while the number of macaroni penguins had actually increased. The scientists of the British Antarctic Survey (BAS) explain the "alarming" decline of the first group by climate change. The diet of chinstrap penguins consists mainly of krill: small shrimp-like creatures. "Because the water warmed, the krill disappeared to the south," says BAS scientist Norman Ratcliffe to the BBC . "Due to the sea ice in the south and the absence of suitable islands to nest, the chinstraps cannot follow their food." The fact that the macaroni penguins are doing well is presumably because they have a more varied diet; those animals also eat fish and shellfish. Other explanations The researchers also looked at other possible explanations for the decline of the chinstrap penguin, such as the volcanic eruption on Zavodovski Island in 2016 and the competition from other hunters of krill, such as the macaroni penguins, whales and the fishing industry. These alternative explanations turned out not to be tenable. The chinstrap penguins also occur on other islands in the Antarctic region. There too, scientists see the numbers declining. The BAS scientists think that the chinstrap penguins will end up on the list of endangered species if the trend continues. Their research can be found in Current Biology .

title: WWF: wildlife populations shrank considerably since 1970, 'but nature restoration is possible'
lead: Populations of birds, mammals, reptiles and other vertebrates have declined by almost three quarters on average since 1970, confirms a biennial report by the World Wildlife Fund. There are large differences, however: half of the studied populations are stable or increasing. The other half is declining, sometimes sharply. A population is a group of animals of the same species living close together. Think of a group of savanna elephants in Zambia or a club of otters in the Weerribben in Overijssel. Most animal species consist of multiple populations that have limited contact with one another. A population can consist of a handful of animals, but also of thousands of individuals. "The most important message of this report is that nature restoration is within reach," says Robert Zwiers, head of impact at the World Wildlife Fund. "Worldwide, wild animals are under severe pressure, but we also see that wild animals worldwide are making a comeback." Otters and sharks Examples of success stories are the tiger, the green sea turtle, the bluefin tuna and the otter in the Netherlands, says Zwiers. "In the Netherlands, otters were extinct. Thanks to cleaner water, connecting habitats and reintroducing otters, they are doing well here again. The bluefin tuna is now no longer threatened by quotas for catching it." Sharks and rays, on the other hand, are declining sharply, says Zwiers. "Many species grow slowly and have few young, which makes them vulnerable. They are caught and also regularly end up as bycatch in fishing nets. Existing agreements are not sufficient to protect these species." 5790 species The World Wildlife Fund bases its conclusions on data from 5790 different species of mammals, birds, amphibians, reptiles and fish. It looked at 35,803 populations around the world for this. Species such as insects, jellyfish and crabs are therefore not included in the study. For each population, the researchers determined the trend since 1970: did the population increase, shrink, or remain stable? Half of the populations shrank, 7 percent of the populations remained stable and the remaining 43 percent of the populations actually grew. Yet the average comes out negative with a decline of 73 percent. According to Zwiers, this is because the shrinking populations shrink faster than the growing populations grow. Repetition of study The figures are not surprising. The previous edition of the Living Planet Report from 2024 also established that the average size of monitored wildlife populations worldwide declined by 73 percent since 1970. "You cannot compare those figures one to one because we have now used more data, but this study confirms the earlier picture," says Zwiers. To restore populations that are under pressure, according to him it is necessary, among other things, to produce our food more sustainably, accelerate the energy transition and reduce investments in the financial sector that harm nature.

title: European Court of Auditors warns of rapidly rising EU debt burden
lead: The European Court of Auditors (ECA) is concerned about the growing debt burden of the European Union. That debt has risen in recent years to 740 billion euros. In 2027 the EU debt will probably grow further to 1 trillion (1,000,000,000,000) euros. That increase in debt is mainly due to support for Ukraine, rising interest rates, defence spending and the corona recovery fund. That fund was created in 2020 to shore up the economic crisis caused by the corona pandemic. From that corona recovery fund, more than 112 billion euros in recovery payments still have to be paid out. Brussels wants to shape part of the EU multiannual budget (2028-2034) in the same way as the corona recovery fund. That means that costs are not reimbursed afterwards but countries receive money in advance if they submit their plans. In those plans they must make clear how they want to achieve EU goals. The Court of Auditors says in its annual report that such a multiannual budget based on the corona recovery fund entails risks. EU countries were allowed in the corona recovery fund to relax or limit plans without providing convincing reasons and evidence for doing so. That carried the risk that countries received EU money for delivering fewer results than had been promised in advance. The Court of Auditors considers this system of submitting plans in advance 'too vague' and 'impossible to check'. For example, the Court of Auditors found irregularities of 45.5 billion euros in the EU accounts for 2025. This concerned, among other things, persistent problems with member states' control systems.

title: Software pioneer of first moon landing Margaret Hamilton (90) died
lead: Margaret Hamilton, who developed the software for the first moon landing of Apollo 11 in 1969, has died. Through her pioneering work in the field of software development, the Americans were able to fly to the moon with Apollo and land there. With this landing the Americans won the space race in the 1960s. Hamilton died on 30 September at the age of 90. Her death was announced by MIT (Massachusetts Institute of Technology), the institute where she worked for many years. Hamilton joined MIT in 1959 and continued to work there until the mid-1970s. Initially to develop software to better predict the weather. At that time computer science was not an official subject and programmers learned the work in practice. Hamilton too taught herself to program. Later Hamilton ended up with the research group that worked on the software for the Apollo program. This department secured a contract with NASA in 1961. Ultimately she led a team of one hundred engineers that designed the software for controlling NASA's Apollo missions. Hamilton is regarded as one of the founders of the field of software engineering. A term she herself devised. Professor Oliver Weck of MIT's Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics says of Hamilton: "To say that she was a pioneer and that she was far ahead of her time would be an enormous understatement. She was a software engineer at a time when this field was still in its infancy; she not only developed advanced code herself, but also led a team that used this emerging technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity has ever produced." In 2016 Hamilton was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom by President Barack Obama for her contribution to science and space travel. In 2017 Margaret Hamilton spoke in an interview about her experiences during the Apollo project:

title: Report: deliberately created crisis makes recovery impossible for Gazans
lead: Three years after the start of the devastating war in Gaza, Palestinians are trapped in a cycle of displacement and violence, with barely any access to food, clean drinking water and care, says Doctors of the World. The overall health of the Palestinian population is steadily deteriorating with irreversible damage as a result. Doctors of the World provides primary care in Gaza and has mapped out the impact of the war and the Israeli blockade of humanitarian aid in a report. The aid organization speaks of a genocide. For example, 97 percent of the Palestinian population is displaced. Nearly half have been displaced between five or ten times and one in five even more than ten times, according to the report. Doctors of the World surveyed 416 widows, pregnant women, breastfeeding women and caregivers of children under 5 years old for the study. Diseases Due to the displacement, Palestinians end up in overcrowded and unsafe shelters without access to, for example, clean drinking water and hygiene facilities. The population is therefore extremely vulnerable to diseases that spread quickly. According to the report, 84 percent of children under 5 years old were ill in the three months preceding the study. They suffered from, among other things, diarrhea and skin conditions. Among pregnant women that was 57 percent. Nearly all pregnant women and breastfeeding women had symptoms of anemia, according to the report. Attack on healthcare facilities Palestinians have barely any access to care because the healthcare system has completely collapsed, says Doctors of the World. The organization says that despite the ceasefire that has been in effect since last October, the attacks on the healthcare system continue. Between January and August, according to the report, there were 45 attacks on, among other things, healthcare facilities. In those attacks, ten aid workers were killed and dozens of others were injured. Three clinics of the aid organization were forced to relocate in recent years due to Israeli attacks. The Israeli blockade of medical aid also causes major shortages in healthcare. Combating diseases that are easy to cure is difficult because there is little or no medication. Due to the dire situation, more and more Palestinians need psychosocial care. According to the report, the number of people who need psychological help has more than doubled in recent years to a million in 2025. According to the aid organization, that help is barely available due to the destruction of the healthcare system in Gaza. Doctors of the World sees that structural food insecurity is a source of fear for almost the entire Palestinian population. 84 percent of Palestinians find it very difficult to get nutritious food. Palestinians have become dependent on community kitchens and soup kitchens of aid organizations. People skip meals or reduce their portions to be able to feed their children, for example, the report states. Food diversity is also low. Israel mainly allows food with a low nutritional value and little protein, says Doctors of the World. As a result, people have a shortage of iron, zinc and essential fatty acids that are too present in meat, fish, nuts and seeds. A shortage of calories and nutrients has major consequences for the recovery process and the development of children. This year alone, the aid organization has treated more than 450 children and 1500 pregnant women and breastfeeding women for malnutrition. Reconstruction Doctors of the World says that the "deliberately created crisis" makes it impossible for Palestinians to recover physically and mentally. The NGO calls on governments to stop the Israeli war violence in Gaza and to ensure that constant emergency aid is admitted, so that Palestinians can recover and rebuild their lives.

title: Drought worsens problems with foundations, nearly half a million homes threatened
lead: The autumn weather seems to really make its entrance today, but the extreme drought of the past months will trouble the Netherlands for a long time. Construction companies that repair foundations also have their hands full with it. More people are raising the alarm because they discovered cracks in the wall after their holiday. It is expected that many more homes could suffer damage in the coming years due to problems with their foundation. Extreme weather conditions due to climate change can worsen those problems. Soil subsidence expert Otto Levelt of knowledge institute Deltares thinks that people with a house with a shallow foundation on clay soil can expect some damage in this period. "For example, 2018 was very dry and then we also saw more problems arise in those areas." Due to drought, the clay soil shrinks and with a shallow foundation that shrinking can continue to below the house. This can cause cracks in walls, or a window or door can start to jam. Nearly half a million homes Deltares monitors in a few places in the Netherlands what happens in the clay, such as in <entity id="org:gemeente-arnhem">Arnhem</entity>. There are some neighborhoods with foundation problems. The costs can rise to tens of thousands of euros . In Arnhem and other municipalities, counters have therefore been opened to help residents, but prevention is even better, says Levelt. There are also many houses on piles and peat and sand soil that have to deal with subsidence. Deltares calculated together with research institute <entity id="org:zbo-nederlandse-organisatie-voor-toegepast-natuurwetenschappelijk-onderzoek">TNO</entity> that 425,000 homes have problems with the foundation or could get them within a short time. Kennis Centrum Aanpak Funderingsproblematiek (KCAF) expects that this number will have risen to approximately 687,000 buildings in about thirty years due to climate change. That means a dark cloud hangs over the housing market. Since 1 April, valuation reports for the sale of a house must contain an indication of how the foundation is doing. Only people often do not know what the real state of their foundation is. In the report it often remains at that indication, based on the location of the house. Changing climate "We think houses should get a kind of housing passport," says director Frank van Lier of KCAF. "With that, people can find out everything about their house." He sees that homeowners bury their heads in the sand when it comes to foundation problems. "While 30 percent of the houses with these problems could be saved with prevention." Soil subsidence expert Levelt sees that much is still possible. "Only then we must build climate-proof." Clay soil can, for example, be covered to prevent drying out. "We also think that drip irrigation around the house can help to keep it moist. Deeper foundations are of course also very important." Levelt points out that prolonged drought, alternating with heavy showers, is more often to be expected due to climate change. For all kinds of houses that is a problem. "A shallowly founded house sinks ever closer to the groundwater with a soft subsoil." It can lead to moisture problems and mold, or flooding if a lot of rain falls. Reaching into the wallet If the groundwater level becomes too low, houses on piles can also stand dry for too long. Then pile rot can occur, which ultimately makes the houses unstable. It is only difficult to influence the groundwater level under your house. In addition, tenants remain dependent on their housing corporation or private landlord to tackle foundation problems. Politics must therefore intervene, KCAF and Vereniging Eigen Huis believe. Vereniging Eigen Huis believes that homeowners should receive support. "Of course the government cannot always reach into the wallet, but the uncertainty is now very great due to the costs that come to some people," says Simon Vrijsen of the interest group. "As a homeowner you have no influence on the causes and you cannot insure yourself against it either." The <entity id="org:zbo-stichting-autoriteit-financiele-markten">Autoriteit Financiële Markten</entity> previously calculated what the total costs are if all homes with foundation problems are repaired. That amounts to more than 11 billion euros. Some of the homeowners can pay this themselves, for example by increasing the mortgage, but about 75,000 of them cannot.

title: Will Trump get the Nobel Prize now? Rather someone who can resist him, experts say
lead: In Norway, it will be announced tomorrow who will receive this year's Nobel Peace Prize. That is most likely already decided, but regardless of who becomes the winner, it will raise eyebrows in the White House. The American president will not receive the peace prize, is the expectation. Last year, President Trump declared himself the rightful winner. The Nobel Prize was, however, awarded to the Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado for "her tireless efforts to promote democratic rights for the people of Venezuela". The White House criticized the Nobel Committee because it would have let "politics go before peace". Trump claimed that he had ended "eight wars" and that therefore only he deserved the prize. Later, Machado still offered her prize to Trump during a visit to the White House, shortly after the US had captured the Venezuelan president Maduro. The Nobel Institute responded that a Nobel Prize cannot be withdrawn, shared or passed on to others. War with Iran This year, Trump has been remarkably quiet in the run-up to the announcement. According to news agency Reuters, he would have been nominated by Cambodia, Israel and Pakistan. Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu also nominated Trump last year. Historian and geopolitical analyst Ivo van de Wijdeven sees no great chance of the peace prize for the American president. "The ceasefire between Hamas and Israel that was negotiated last year has indeed held, but there is not really peace yet," he says. Moreover, Trump himself started the war against Iran earlier this year. "One of the criteria is that you must promote peace." The winner of the peace prize has been highly controversial a number of times. For example, the American Secretary of State Henry Kissinger (1923-2023) won the prize in 1973 for "jointly negotiating a ceasefire in Vietnam" together with the Vietnamese politician Le Duc Tho, who refused the prize. Two members of the committee resigned and The New York Times called it the Nobel War Prize. Kissinger was responsible for heavy bombardments in North Vietnam and Laos and supported the bloody coup in Chile in the same year. How is the winner of the Nobel Peace Prize chosen? The winner of the Nobel Peace Prize is chosen by the Norwegian Nobel Committee . Its members are in turn selected by the Storting (the Norwegian parliament) for a term of six years, and can be re-elected. The committee consists of Norwegian citizens. Winners must be nominated. Worldwide there are tens of thousands of people who have the right to nominate people, such as rectors of universities, certain professors, leaders of peace research institutes and institutes for international relations, parliamentarians, members of the International Criminal Court and former winners of the peace prize The deadline for nominations is 31 January. Then the five-member Nobel Committee reviews all nominations and makes a selection. That is assessed by independent experts. The committee makes a final decision during the last meeting before the announcement. That happens on the basis of four main areas: arms control and disarmament, peace negotiations, democracy and human rights. It is not yet clear who will be eligible for the prize this year. Nominations are not made public by the committee, the full list of names is only made public after fifty years. Haakon Gjerloew, acting director of the Peace Research Institute Oslo, tells news agency Reuters that he expects someone will be chosen who can resist the pressure of Trump. He mentions as examples Pope Leo, the International Criminal Court, the International Court of Justice and Francesca Albanese, the special UN rapporteur for the occupied Palestinian territories. Historian Van de Wijdeven does not see it happening that the committee lets the choice be influenced by Trump. He expects that the committee will send a message to focus attention on 'forgotten' conflicts. "When the prize was given to Machado last year, that was also a signal to people about a conflict that many people had forgotten. You see that more often with the Nobel Prize awards." Van de Wijdeven sees Sudan's Emergency Response Rooms as a possible winner. These are networks built by local people that provide humanitarian aid in the Sudan war, which is also called the largest crisis in the world, but receives relatively little attention. According to Van de Wijdeven, that would be in line with the tradition of the Nobel Committee, which often chooses "unknowns and unloved ones".

title: Rabbits must make growth in Rotterdam port possible again
lead: The port of Rotterdam must get rid of the 'nitrogen lock' and receives 50 million euros from <entity id="org:kabinet">het kabinet</entity> for this. This must pay for nature restoration next year, so that construction and other permits can be issued again. The industrial expansion of one of the largest and most modern ports in the world must be saved with, among other things, releasing rabbits in nature areas, combating exotic plants and insects, and limiting the number of cyclists and walkers along the coast. This is stated in the 'Routekaart naar natuurvergunningverlening in de Rotterdamse Haven' by, among others, the national government, the <entity id="org:gemeente-rotterdam">gemeente Rotterdam</entity> and the port company. It is one of the 'area-oriented plans' with which <entity id="person:jaimi-van-essen">minister Van Essen</entity> wants to tackle the nitrogen problem. "All together it ensures that we can start issuing permits again," says Arne Weverling (VVD), deputy of the <entity id="org:provincie-zuid-holland">provincie Zuid-Holland</entity>. "There are companies that do have plans but no longer even dare to apply for a permit. We say: submit your plans again. Come to Rotterdam." Meijendel and Westduinpark This concerns nature restoration in Natura2000 areas. These are Meijendel and Berkheide between <entity id="org:gemeente-s-gravenhage">Den Haag</entity> and <entity id="org:gemeente-katwijk">Katwijk</entity>, the Hague Westduinpark and Wapendal, Solleveld and Kapittelduinen between Den Haag, <entity id="org:gemeente-westland">Westland</entity> and Hoek van Holland and Voornes Duin on the island of Voorne-<entity id="org:gemeente-putten">Putten</entity>. In part of the areas drinking water is extracted. The areas are professionally managed, among others by dune water company Dunea. And nitrogen deposition is not necessarily the biggest problem there. Water management and coastal protection, for example, are just as important to maintain nature. It is therefore relatively easy in these locations to achieve preservation of biodiversity and other Natura2000 objectives. The plan states that rabbits will be released for a "robust dune ecosystem that is resistant to nitrogen deposition". The dunes must be able to drift and for that, maintenance of the vegetation is necessary. Rabbits do that, but their population has declined sharply due to infectious diseases. What does the port of Rotterdam have to do with mainly Hague walking areas?, is the question to alderman Tim Versnel (VVD), who is responsible for the port of Rotterdam. "In such a small densely populated country you almost always have to deal with each other," he answers. "We are a team Netherlands together and we must ensure together that we move forward again." Cooperation nature organizations The port of Rotterdam must also take measures itself, such as closer cooperation between the business community and nature organizations, more electrically powered equipment in the port and ships that emit less. Versnel calls the agreements an important first step. "We want to be the most sustainable and strongest port in 2050. That is not succeeding now. It will still take some effort but we are heading in the right direction." The Rotterdam Port Authority, the municipality and the province of Zuid-Holland have been raising the alarm for years about the nitrogen problems that endanger economic activities in the port area. Precisely greening projects are at a standstill because no permits can be granted. Economic growth The port does not only suffer from the nitrogen problem. A third of all sustainable projects have been delayed due to capacity problems on the electricity grid. Due to all the delays, the investment climate has deteriorated. The port company has also warned about a shortage of space given the many projects that are planned. Such as its own terminal for defense and landing of new wind farms. The construction of a new nuclear power plant has now been cancelled. But the port of Rotterdam is still in the picture for small reactors, the so-called SMRs. The restoration of the Natura2000 areas is therefore only the beginning.

title: Freight rates for large crude oil tankers rise to record level
lead: Freight rates for crude oil tankers have reached a record high. Demand for tankers is high, but worldwide there is a shortage. That appears from research by ING. "Due to the ongoing war in Iran and disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, tankers have to cover greater distances," says ING economist Rico Luman. Tankers are therefore underway longer and can be deployed less often. In addition, oil flows from the Middle East are starting to get going again, which leads to the extra demand, Luman explains. Attacks Last week, most tankers were attacked since the start of the war against Iran, reports the Maritime Information Center (JMIC), which is under US leadership. Attempted attacks are also included; as well as intimidation with, for example, drones flying over. Last week, the number of ships that sailed through the Strait of Hormuz fell to the lowest level in two months. Only seven ships made the crossing. Oil exports from the Strait therefore also declined. Under the radar The actual oil flows from the Middle East cannot be fully seen in the official figures, economist Luman says. Part happens under the radar, under the protection of the US army. "They use shuttle services of tankers that sail through the Strait of Hormuz and then reload the cargo onto other ships." According to the economist, the dollar also has an effect on the record high of the freight rates. The dollar has risen against the euro. "On the world market, crude oil is traded in US dollars by standard, so now you need more euros." Money like water At the start of this month, renting one tanker cost an average of 500,000 dollars per day. That is ten times the average of last year. "Earlier peaks, such as in 2022 after the invasion of Ukraine, were above 100,000 dollars. But like now, we have never seen that before," says economist Luman. According to him, those prices on routes from or towards the Middle East are much higher still. And that therefore also concerns the revenues of tanker shipping companies. "They are now making money like water." For years, little has been invested in crude oil tankers. "Especially during the corona crisis, there was less driving and flying," economist Luman explains. Now that demand has increased again, orders are also increasing again. But many ships will not be delivered until 2028 at the earliest. Probably after the current rise is over. Consumers also have to be patient for a while. Although the oil price has fallen somewhat again recently, the petrol and diesel price remains high. "That is because there is little refining capacity, which has been damaged in the Middle East and also in Russia. On top of that, we are dealing with very high transport costs of tankers. That keeps the fuel price at the pump higher than you would expect," Luman concludes.

title: Tropical storm Isaias has grown into the first hurricane of the Atlantic season
lead: Tropical storm Isaias has grown into the first hurricane of the Atlantic season in the Gulf of Mexico. The expectation of the American National Hurricane Center is that the hurricane will make landfall late tomorrow evening or early Saturday morning, although it is still unclear where. The states most at risk are Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama and Florida. The warm water of the Gulf of Mexico contributes to the rapid intensification of the hurricane. Until now, the Atlantic hurricane season was very quiet due to a strong El Niño. The winds that El Niño causes make the formation of tropical storms difficult. Isaias is therefore the first hurricane of the season. Life-threatening The center of the hurricane was observed yesterday evening about 745 kilometers south of Mississippi and was moving at 15 kilometers per hour, with speeds around it of 120 kilometers per hour. Together with heavy rainfall, that can cause sudden flooding. For the four southern states on the Gulf Coast, the National Hurricane Center has issued a warning for a possible storm surge. Especially the southern parts of Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama and Florida are at risk. The weather institute speaks of a "life-threatening storm surge". More than thirty million people live in the four states. Power outages and evacuations These residents must follow the advice of the local authorities, according to the American hurricane institute. They must also take into account prolonged power outages and possible evacuations. Hundreds of kilometers inland, heavy wind gusts and severe rainfall are also still expected.

title: Construction company BAM buys specialist in transport pipelines and heat networks for half a billion
lead: Construction company BAM is taking over A.Hak, a specialist in the field of underground infrastructure. The large Dutch construction company is paying 504 million euros for it. A.Hak is a major player in the field of constructing heat networks, laying kilometres-long transport pipelines and bringing energy generated at sea ashore. The company from Geldermalsen does this mainly in the Netherlands, but also in Belgium and the United Kingdom. Last year the company made almost 18 million euros in profit. Strengthening BAM CEO Ruud Joosten calls the takeover a big step in the construction company's growth strategy. According to Joosten, it ensures that BAM spreads its work even better across the whole Netherlands. He also expects a lot from the company's growth in the United Kingdom because of the construction of water and energy infrastructure. "We are pleased that A.Hak will continue to play a central role in the further development of BAM's work in the field of energy and underground infrastructure," says Henk Herremans, CEO of A.Hak. The CEO speaks of new opportunities for customers and employees. Around 900 full-time employees work at A. Hak. The company expects that all employees will continue to be badly needed given the major task of the energy transition. A.Hak will continue to operate under its own name. Construction With the takeover, Koninklijke BAM Groep B.V. strengthens its position as the largest construction company in the Netherlands. Last year the company earned more than 7 billion euros from construction contracts and saw its profit nearly triple to 211 million euros. The construction sector has faced challenges in recent years such as nitrogen restrictions, staff shortages and uncertainty about construction projects. Relatively many construction companies stopped after the corona period, but large contractors such as BAM, Heijmans and Dura Vermeer are actually receiving many orders.

title: Saudi Arabia: dead and wounded from Houthi attack, launch platform destroyed
lead: In attacks by the Houthis yesterday on airports in Saudi Arabia, three people were killed, and 36 people were also injured. According to the Saudi authorities, a Moroccan and an Algerian woman died in an attack on the airport of Abha, in the south of the country near the border of Yemen. In an attack on the airport of Riyadh, a Sudanese man was killed. In a response, the military coalition in Yemen led by Saudi Arabia attacked 82 military targets, including a launch platform for ballistic missiles. That platform was used for the attacks on the airports. The Houthis in Yemen claim that they carried out a new attack on the airport of the Saudi capital Riyadh. The group calls on airlines to no longer operate flights in Saudi airspace. Saudi Arabia has not yet confirmed the attack. Fighting in Yemen Two days ago, attacks were also already carried out on Saudi airports. Last month, the ceasefire between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthis, which came about in 2022, was broken by an offensive by the Houthis. They gained control in Yemen of the entire area along the Red Sea, including the important strait Bab al-Mandab. From that area, military complexes and oil installations in Saudi Arabia are attacked. Earlier this week, the Yemeni government army began a counteroffensive. According to the Minister of Information, Bab al-Mandab was recaptured. A spokesperson for the Houthis told the BBC that the attacks on the airports in Saudi Arabia are a response "to the Saudi aggression against our country, which has experienced no fewer than sixty air and missile attacks in the past 24 hours". Due to the situation in Yemen, around 200,000 Yemenis have fled. The UN organization for migration and aid to refugees (IOM) called on donor countries yesterday to take action.

title: Trade confrontation looms: 'super crucial' meeting between EU and China
lead: Today and tomorrow Beijing is the setting for a meeting between the European Union and China. After months of rising tensions over mutual trade, European Commissioner for Trade Sefcovic meets there with Chinese Trade Minister Wang Wentao. The European Union wants a solution as quickly as possible for an increasingly skewed trade balance that has now risen to 1 billion euros per day. As a result, European industry and employment are being hit hard. Sefcovic calls this meeting "super crucial". China, on the other hand, benefits from the status quo, because it earns a lot from European consumers. An ever larger part of China's economic growth must come from exports, because the economy is faltering at home. Sharper tone The tone of the European Union has become increasingly sharp in recent months. In her annual speech to the European Parliament, Commission President Von der Leyen emphasized that the EU-China dialogue must yield concrete results. Otherwise the EU will "use all the means at our disposal to bring the relationship into balance". The EU accuses China of unfair trade practices, such as state aid and artificially keeping the Chinese currency low. European companies cannot compete with that. If this meeting yields insufficient in the eyes of the EU, trade measures may follow. These could consist of levies or even restrictions on the import of Chinese products. No need to accommodate In China there is little sympathy for European concerns. China points to the strength of its own industry: efficient supply chains; modern factories and cheap logistics that ensure packages reach customers in Europe quickly. But that is only part of the story. Across the board, European companies do not get the same access to the Chinese market as Chinese companies in Europe. Chinese companies can also easily get cheap loans or subsidies and the Chinese government helps them with free land or business premises. China thinks it does not need to accommodate the EU. Beijing sees the EU as a weak and divided player and thinks it can make as few concessions as possible by playing member states off against each other. That is a strategy China uses more often. When the European Commission wanted to impose levies on Chinese electric cars last year, China came with levies on French cognac. In this way China put pressure on France not to cooperate with the levies on electric cars. If the EU comes with measures in the coming weeks, China will now undoubtedly also come with a counterattack. The European commitment The EU hopes to make agreements with China about limiting exports to Europe, for example of hybrid cars. The EU also wants better access to the Chinese market for European producers. If China is not prepared to conclude a trade deal, additional import levies will come in sectors where Chinese dominance is too great, the EU threatens. In addition, Germany and France, the most powerful countries of the EU, have devised a more far-reaching instrument. With it, it must become possible to deny China access to the EU internal market more quickly than now. That Germany also supports this is telling. The country was always cautious in tackling China, out of fear that German industry would be hit by Chinese countermeasures. Focus is next week Next week trade commissioner Sefcovic will present the results of his meeting to the EU government leaders, when they are in Brussels for an EU summit. Then it must become clear whether the EU is indeed prepared to take tough measures, even if they hurt in Europe because prices rise as a result. Experts urge taking those measures, because the economic consequences of doing nothing are greater. The coming weeks must show whether the EU follows the advice, or whether China is proven right and the EU remains too divided to take tough action.

title: More room to negotiate for buyers, but housing market still tight
lead: Although there is more room for home buyers to negotiate, the tightness on the housing market persists. That is the conclusion of the estate agents' association NVM. In the past quarter, affiliated estate agents sold 41,700 existing homes, roughly the same as a year ago. Because of the summer holidays, there are always fewer transactions in the third quarter. This quarter the decline was larger than normal. An existing home cost an average of 503,000 euros. Prices are rising by almost 2 percent per year. "The market remains tight: almost two thirds of sales are still overbid", says Lana Goutsmits-Gerssen, chair of the NVM. Greater supply of purchases at the expense of rentals In the past quarter, 48,500 homes were put up for sale by NVM estate agents, 5 percent more than a year earlier. The growth is mainly in apartments, with former rental homes coming up for sale. "More supply gives home buyers a little more breathing room", says Goutsmits-Gerssen. "They can schedule a second viewing more often and get more room to negotiate on some homes." At the same time, the supply for tenants shrank. New-build homes hard to sell The supply of new-build homes rose by 17 percent compared with a year earlier. As a result, the supply of new homes is approaching the highest level in more than ten years. The higher supply did not translate into more homes sold. The NVM reports that affiliated estate agents actually sold 400 fewer homes this quarter than a year earlier. "Long construction times and high bridging costs make the step more difficult", says Goutsmits-Gerssen. "Homes must match what people are looking for and can afford." The average price of a new-build home has also passed the half-million mark since the start of 2026. Since then the price has remained roughly the same. Because the price per square metre does rise, shrinkflation occurs: the buyer gets less living space for the same price.

title: Removed uteruses and testicles: 'old transgender law caused deep human suffering'
lead: The Dutch <entity id="org:regering">regering</entity> already offered apologies in 2021 for the transgender law that was in force between 1985 and 2014. Now the research report Een onmenselijke wet , carried out by researchers from Radboud University, shows how deep the suffering was for the people who had to deal with the law. The researchers, who started work on behalf of the Ministry of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-onderwijs-cultuur-en-wetenschap">Onderwijs, Cultuur en Wetenschap</entity>, interviewed 28 transgender and intersex persons who paint a picture of the physical, psychological and social damage they suffered because of the law. The transgender law comprised the rules that people had to meet before they were allowed to change their registered sex. Removing testicles and uterus For example, they first had to be made irreversibly infertile, which meant the uterus and ovaries or the testicles had to be removed, and they had to be unmarried, which forced some to divorce. An expert statement from a doctor and psychologist also had to be submitted. Marloes Hülsken, researcher at Radboud University and one of the authors of the report, says that all this has left deep marks, especially the requirement of irreversible infertility. Hülsken: "Interviewees spoke about the enormous impact of this on their lives: it affected the desire to have children and biological parenthood, forced operations and stopped the production of the body's own hormones. For some of those affected, this immediately caused a feeling of grief and pain, for others the realisation of the impact sometimes came only years later." 'As if I were a criminal' Because of the barriers erected for changing sex registration, people often lived for many years with incorrect official documents. According to researchers, this had major consequences for people in daily life. The report cites Carlo Weide. He tells how he had a gun pointed at him during a pat-down at an airport in Greece. "As if I were a criminal, only because my photo matched my head, but what was in my passport did not, the V." Ron de Vries tells about his experience: "What struck me most was that everyone thought it was normal that it is okay to sterilise a young person, because that person may not have offspring. And if you say something about that, then you are the one who is not normal." Man or woman was determined The researchers also write that people who were born without the medically customary definition of man or woman, and for whom it was determined whether they were a man or a woman, fell under the transgender law for a sex change later in life. "And thus under the same drastic requirements." The government apologised in 2021, after which it was promised that additional research would follow. "This research gives a voice to the transgender and intersex people who were affected by the old law", said <entity id="person:judith-tielen">staatssecretaris Tielen</entity> of Onderwijs, Cultuur en Wetenschap. "Their stories show how much pain they have experienced."

title: RTL: chaos at alimony organization, employees speak of culture of fear
lead: Things are not going well at the government agency <entity id="org:zbo-landelijk-bureau-inning-onderhoudsbijdragen">LBIO</entity>, an organization that helps people with mediation for child and partner alimony. That is what RTL Nieuws writes after its own investigation. Employees of the LBIO speak of a socially unsafe working atmosphere and a "culture of fear", causing more and more people to report sick. As a result, the waiting time to help parents is increasing. State Secretary <entity id="person:claudia-van-bruggen">Claudia van Bruggen</entity> of Justice acknowledges the problems. She sent a letter to <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity> last night. It also states that the Labour Inspectorate has started an investigation. According to RTL, the parliamentary letter was sent after the news broadcaster had asked the ministry questions about the chaotic situation within the organization. The Landelijk Bureau Inning Onderhoudsbijdragen (LBIO) mediates free of charge when an ex-partner pays no or too little alimony. In 2024, mediation succeeded in 75 percent of the requests, preventing extra costs and further escalation. That year the organization helped about six thousand people, according to the annual report . 47 percent absenteeism RTL Nieuws spoke with eleven current and former employees. The problems would mainly pile up in the intervention team, which is concerned with getting overdue alimony started. The department has an absenteeism rate of 47 percent, according to absenteeism figures RTL has seen. On its website, the LBIO reports that there are longer waiting times than usual, which can last weeks. An employee who has been employed longer calls the waiting times "extreme". Employees paint a picture that people who raise the alarm sometimes urgently need help to pay their bills and get into trouble because of the waiting times. "Parents who ask us for help and may not have money to buy food for their children, it gives me such a stomach ache", RTL quotes an employee. Several employees sent an urgent letter to the Ministry of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-justitie-en-veiligheid">Justitie en Veiligheid</entity> last summer, to make their concerns known. The letter is in RTL's possession. The employees write about the high workload, the backlogs and the absenteeism. A culture of fear is also mentioned. "We are sending this letter anonymously and by post, because we do not feel safe to make our name known. (...) Colleagues feel ignored, excluded, intimidated and no longer dare to speak out", the letter states. Jacobine Geel The urgent letter also contains firm accusations against interim director Jacobine Geel. The problems would have increased due to her arrival. They also state that Geel "addressed the team with the high absenteeism in a harsh and intimidating manner". At a meeting on 2 July, Geel would have said that "the sick must come back quickly or look for a new job". In the letter, which was sent on 8 July, the employees ask for a new director. RTL Nieuws is in possession of audio recordings of closed staff meetings. According to the news broadcaster, these show that Geel calls the workload in the intervention department "screamingly high". She would also have said that the amount of overdue work is "actually no longer manageable" and that action is being taken to get the situation "back under control and calm it down".
